topics.title: History by numbers
topics.intro: How long ago? How many died? Historians need maths to measure time and change, including the tricky jump from BC to AD.
topics.teach: Explain why there is no year 0, and what that does to BC–AD sums.
topics.talk: Ask her how many years ago the Battle of Hastings was.
topics.hook: How long ago or how long for? Take the earlier year from the later one: end − start.

topics.title: Reading historical sources
topics.intro: A source is evidence from the past. Reading one well uses your English skills: tone, word choice and the writer’s purpose. Then historians ask: who wrote it, when, and why?
topics.teach: Explain why a biased source can still be useful to a historian.
topics.talk: Ask her who wrote the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and how that might affect what it says about the Vikings.
topics.hook: Ask **NOP** of every source: its **N**ature, **O**rigin and **P**urpose.

items.prompt: Henry VIII reigned from 1509 to 1547. For about how many years was he king?
items.hook: How long for? End − start: 1547 − 1509 = 38 years.

items.prompt: Elizabeth I was born in 1533 and became queen in 1558. How old was she?
items.explain: 1558 − 1533 = 25. She then reigned for 44 years, until 1603.
items.hook: Age = the later year − the year of birth.

items.prompt: Suppose England’s population fell from about 5 million in 1300 to about 2.5 million in 1400. Roughly what fraction was left?
items.explain: 2.5 is half of 5. Plague returned again and again after 1348, so the population stayed low for a long time.
items.hook: From 5 million to 2.5 million: half is left, 1/2.

items.prompt: Which words show how the writer felt about the raiders?

options.feedback: That describes the warning signs in the sky, not the raiders.

items.explain: “Heathen” (not Christian) and “lamentable havoc” (terrible destruction) show the monks saw the Vikings as godless and the raid as a disaster.
items.passage: This year came dreadful fore-warnings over the land of the Northumbrians, terrifying the people most woefully: these were immense sheets of light rushing through the air, and whirlwinds, and fiery dragons flying across the firmament. These tremendous tokens were soon followed by a great famine: and not long after, … the harrowing inroads of heathen men made lamentable havoc in the church of God in Holy-island, by rapine and slaughter.
items.passageSource: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, entry for AD 793, written by monks (translated by James Ingram, 1823). Holy-island is Lindisfarne.
items.hook: Feelings hide in the describing words: “heathen”, “lamentable”.

items.prompt: Why might the writer begin with the “fiery dragons” in the sky?

options.text: To suggest the raid was a sign from God

options.feedback: People at the time saw strange lights or storms as omens. Historians think these may have been the northern lights.

options.text: To make the story more exciting and funny
options.feedback: Look at the tone: “dreadful”, “terrifying”, “woefully”. It is meant to be frightening.

items.explain: Monks believed God sent signs before disasters. Opening with omens makes the raid feel like a punishment that had been foretold.
items.passage: This year came dreadful fore-warnings over the land of the Northumbrians, terrifying the people most woefully: these were immense sheets of light rushing through the air, and whirlwinds, and fiery dragons flying across the firmament. These tremendous tokens were soon followed by a great famine: and not long after, … the harrowing inroads of heathen men made lamentable havoc in the church of God in Holy-island, by rapine and slaughter.
items.passageSource: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, entry for AD 793, written by monks (translated by James Ingram, 1823). Holy-island is Lindisfarne.
items.hook: In 793 people often read strange skies as warnings from God.

items.prompt: The Chronicle was written by monks. How might that affect what it says about the Vikings?

options.text: As victims, they show the Vikings as cruel heathens
It means the source is completely useless
options.feedback: A one-sided source is still useful: it shows how people at the time felt and what they believed.

options.text: It makes no difference to what they wrote
options.feedback: Who writes a source always matters. Monks were the victims here.

items.explain: The source is biased, but useful: it tells us how terrifying the raids felt to Christians. Historians compare it with other evidence, such as archaeology.
items.passage: This year came dreadful fore-warnings over the land of the Northumbrians, terrifying the people most woefully: these were immense sheets of light rushing through the air, and whirlwinds, and fiery dragons flying across the firmament. These tremendous tokens were soon followed by a great famine: and not long after, … the harrowing inroads of heathen men made lamentable havoc in the church of God in Holy-island, by rapine and slaughter.
items.passageSource: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, entry for AD 793, written by monks (translated by James Ingram, 1823). Holy-island is Lindisfarne.
items.hook: Ask who wrote it: monks, whose fellow monks and churches were the raiders’ targets, were hardly neutral.

items.prompt: Why does Elizabeth call herself “a weak and feeble woman”?

options.text: To turn other people’s doubts upside down
Because she was ill and weak that day
options.feedback: The word “but” tells you she is about to turn the idea around.

options.text: To admit she could not lead the army herself
options.feedback: She is doing the opposite: showing she is a strong leader.

items.explain: This is a contrast. She admits the doubts some people had about a female ruler, then answers them with a powerful image of courage.
items.passage: I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too, and think foul scorn that Parma or Spain, or any prince of Europe, should dare to invade the borders of my realm.
items.passageSource: Elizabeth I, speech to her army at Tilbury as the Spanish Armada approached (1588), as written down years later by Leonel Sharp, a chaplain who was there
items.hook: A clever speaker admits a weakness first, then turns it into a strength.

items.prompt: Which technique is “of a king, and of a king of England too”?

options.text: A simile comparing her to a king
options.feedback: There is no comparison using “like” or “as”.
None of these words imitate a sound.

items.explain: Repeating “of a king” and then adding “of England too” builds up the idea, stirring national pride in her soldiers.
items.passage: I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too, and think foul scorn that Parma or Spain, or any prince of Europe, should dare to invade the borders of my realm.
items.passageSource: Elizabeth I, speech to her army at Tilbury as the Spanish Armada approached (1588), as written down years later by Leonel Sharp, a chaplain who was there
items.hook: Repetition builds a speech to a climax: “of a king, and of a king of England too”.

items.prompt: This version of the speech was written down by someone who heard it, but many years later. What does that mean for historians?

options.text: We can’t be sure these were her exact words
It must be completely made up
options.feedback: He was there, so it is probably close to what she said. It just may not be word for word.

options.text: It is more reliable, as he had time to think
options.feedback: Memories fade and change over time, so a later account is usually less exact.

items.explain: When a source was made, and by whom, affects how far we can trust it. Historians call this its provenance.
items.passage: I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too, and think foul scorn that Parma or Spain, or any prince of Europe, should dare to invade the borders of my realm.
items.passageSource: Elizabeth I, speech to her army at Tilbury as the Spanish Armada approached (1588), as written down years later by Leonel Sharp, a chaplain who was there
items.hook: Written down years later = a memory, not a recording.

items.prompt: A source that gives only one side of the story is…
items.explain: Biased sources are still useful: they show what people believed, and why.
items.hook: Biased = one-sided, like a fan describing their own team’s match.
items.example: An advert for a cereal is biased: it only tells you the good things.

items.answer: who made it, when, and why
items.explain: Asking about provenance helps a historian judge how reliable a source is.
items.hook: Provenance is a source’s back story: **who** made it, **when**, and **why**.
items.example: Antiques experts check provenance too: who owned a painting before, and when.

items.prompt: When historians check one source against others to see if they agree, they are trying to…
items.explain: If several independent sources agree, we can be more confident about what happened.
items.hook: Corroborate = check it with a **co**-witness: do other sources agree?
items.example: Police corroborate a story by asking other witnesses whether they saw the same thing.
